titles.l1: One cubby each, one child each
titles.l4: Perfect pairings, and what size means

kernelIdea: A bijection is injective and surjective: every t has exactly one pre-image. Bijections are how mathematicians compare sizes, including infinite ones.

kernels.l1: If every child has a cubby and every cubby has a child, there are just as many of each — without counting.
kernels.l2: When you can pair up two piles perfectly, with nothing left over on either side, the piles are the same size. You do not have to count them.
kernels.l3: A bijection is a perfect matching: one-to-one and onto at the same time. Two sets have the same size exactly when a bijection between them exists, and this works even for sets too big to count.
kernels.l4: A function is a perfect pairing when it is both one-to-one and onto, so every element of the target has exactly one input sent to it. For finite sets that forces the two to have equal size; for infinite sets, a perfect pairing is what "same size" means.
kernels.l5: A bijection pairs two sets perfectly. Sameness of size is *defined* by the existence of one, which is why the counting numbers and the even numbers turn out to be the same size.
kernels.l6: Bijections are the isomorphisms of Set; the identity is one, and compositions of bijections are bijections.
kernels.l7: A bijection is simultaneously injective and surjective, so every element of the codomain has exactly one pre-image. Equinumerosity is defined by the existence of a bijection, which extends the notion of size to infinite sets.
kernels.l8: Bijections are the isomorphisms of Set and define cardinality; the diagonal argument shows no bijection ℕ → ℝ exists, so infinities come in different sizes.

kernel: A bijection is both injective and surjective: every t has exactly one pre-image. For finite sets, injection ⇒ |S| ≤ |T|, surjection ⇒ |S| ≥ |T|, bijection ⇒ |S| = |T|. Bijections are how mathematicians compare infinite sets.
